name: MATS (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: an AI catastrophe kills people everywhere and the future lost is everyone's, so the result is spread by world population.
summary: MATS (ML Alignment & Theory Scholars, Berkeley and London) trains researchers for AI safety: scholars spend ten weeks on a research project with a mentor from an AI lab or safety group, and many then continue for four months or longer in an extension phase. This model covers all its work in 2024, its first full year as its own charity ($2.2M of programme spending, $2.9M in all, in its Form 990), when about 153 scholars took part (stipends paid by AI Safety Support, a co-funder). At the defaults it averts about 0.8 years of healthy life per $1,000, from 0.07 to 4 on the model's own ranges, so the result is mostly uncertainty: the scholars who go on to work on AI risk because of MATS (25%, our judgment from its alumni data) are valued by their later work at a typical dollar of such work, credited by MATS's share of the resources behind the training (about 3%), and with their research during the programme, the extension's research as a typical project's cut in the forecast risk of an AI catastrophe (Rethink Priorities' cross-cause model, the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament's experts), deaths valued like every death and the future lost counted through the discount rate; the training gives nearly nine tenths of the result, and the next dollar counts at 31.5% of the past average. It is about two thirds of the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy's result, mainly because less of its work is aimed at misuse (10%) and AI Safety Support's stipends and mentors' time lower its share; the biggest swings are the chance of an AI catastrophe (the slider), Rethink's typical cut per dollar for misuse work, the years a cut counts and the missing-data discount, and every branch is discounted for missing data: no outcome of the work on the risk is measured and the alumni survey has no comparison group.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. rows.label: AI: share of the AI spending on work against misuse (dangerous-capability evaluations, defences against misuse)
rows.explainer: Of MATS's research, the share aimed at people using AI to do harm. Scholars by mentor track in the first cohort with a published split (Winter 2024-25, the nearest to 2024): oversight and control 31%, interpretability 23%, evaluations 22%, AI agency 13%, governance 10%. Only part of the evaluations work is about misuse (dangerous-capability evaluations of bio and cyber uplift); much of it tests deception, scheming and situational awareness, which is misalignment work, as are oversight, control, interpretability and agency. About half of evaluations: 10%, our judgment, 3% (evaluations mostly about misalignment) to 20% (all of evaluations and some governance). Below GovAI's and IAPS's 20% and FAR.AI's 28%, whose misuse work is a named team or a named set of papers. The result moves with this share because Rethink Priorities' typical misuse project cuts deaths in survivable catastrophes far more per dollar than its misalignment one.

rows.formula: ((1 - ai_misuse_cost_share) * @catastrophe.ai_extinction_cut_per_million + ai_misuse_cost_share * @catastrophe.ai_misuse_extinction_cut_per_million) * ai_extinction_per_year * deaths_if_extinct + ((1 - ai_misuse_cost_share) * @catastrophe.ai_catastrophe_cut_per_million + ai_misuse_cost_share * @catastrophe.ai_misuse_catastrophe_cut_per_million) * (ai_catastrophe_per_year * ai_deaths_if_catastrophe + ai_smaller_per_year * ai_smaller_deaths)

rows.label: Field-building: share who go on to work on these risks because of it
rows.explainer: Share of the scholars who go on to work on AI risk because of MATS. MATS says 75% of its alumni now work in AI alignment, transparency and security (home page); its survey of the first four cohorts (72 respondents, 46% of alumni) found 78% working or researching on alignment, 1.4% on capabilities. Many would have got there anyway: asked what they would have done that winter without MATS, 24% said independent research without a mentor and 13% with one, several answers allowed (Winter 2023-24 retrospective), and the survey covers only the 2021-23 cohorts, with no comparison group; only 8% said MATS did not contribute to their job progression. As GovAI's alumni in a role (60%) times the share of their later work the programme brought about (about a third), 75% × about a third ≈ 25%, our judgment, 8% (response bias, most would have entered) to 45% (MATS the main route in for many).

rows.explainer: The research phase in Berkeley: ten weeks in Winter 2023-24 (8 January to 15 March 2024; the retrospective), the same in Summer 2024 (its page: a 10-week research phase in Berkeley).

rows.label: Field-building: the scholars' research during the programme, as a share of a typical work-year's value
rows.explainer: What a week of a scholar's mentored research during the programme is worth against a week of typical AI safety work at its full cost (@catastrophe.cost_per_work_year), net of the research some would have done anyway that winter. Early-career work, but mentored and the programme's stated output (some became papers at top venues): about a third of a typical week, our judgment; times about three quarters for those who would otherwise have done alignment research anyway (24% of the Winter 2023-24 cohort said independent research without a mentor, 13% with one, several answers allowed): 25%, 10% to 50%.

rows.label: Field-building: the scholars' research during the programme, in dollars of typical work
rows.explainer: Scholars × the research phase in years × its value against a typical work-year × the shared cost of a work-year: about $1.8M at the best guesses. Its resources are the training's (MATS's cost, the stipends that pay for the scholars' time, mentors), so MATS's credit is fb_attribution_share, applied with the branch's other adjustments; it isn't in fb_credit_share, which shares the alumni's later work with their employers.

rows.label: Field-building: the training's share of the credit for that work
rows.explainer: The employers pay for the alumni's work itself, so the training gets credit by share of resources: everything spent on the training (MATS's cost and the co-funders') over that plus the alumni's added work (fb_work_dollars), computed so it moves with its inputs; MATS's own part of the training's resources is fb_attribution_share. At the best guesses about $3.8M against about $44M (153 × 25% × five discounted years at the shared $250,000 a work-year), about 8%.

Deaths averted that are in a COVID-scale pandemic (a part of deaths_averted)
rows.explainer: A natural or zoonotic pandemic on COVID's scale kills mostly older people, so its deaths are valued at COVID-19's age mix; every other size (a catastrophe that kills a share of the world, extinction) at the world's. A policy or field-building branch pointed at the pandemic area adds its deaths averted × bio_covid_scale_share here. Fixed.

AI field work: share of the research that bears on catastrophic risk

source.title: MATS mentor selection (LessWrong, 10 January 2025)
source.quote: Oversight & control: 24 scholars (31%)

rows.explainer: Nearly all MATS research is aimed at risks from advanced AI: scholars by mentor track in Winter 2024-25 were oversight and control 31%, interpretability 23%, evaluations 22%, AI agency 13% and governance 10% (MATS mentor selection); a little is about nearer harms (bias, everyday misuse) or is general ML work, valued in unmodelled_benefits_adj. 90%, our judgment, 80% to 100%, above GovAI's and IAPS's 80% whose policy work covers competitiveness and economics.

rows.label: AI field work: uptake against a typical project

source.title: MATS, Summer 2024 programme page
source.quote: won best paper at ICML 2024

rows.explainer: The alumni's research in the extension phase against Rethink Priorities' typical small AI project. Above typical in output: mentored by researchers at Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Redwood Research and Apollo Research, MATS projects have become papers at top venues (a best paper at ICML 2024 on debate, NeurIPS workshop papers on manipulation by models trained on user feedback); MATS's home page counts 'more than 240 research publications' and 'over 23,000 collective citations' across all cohorts. Below in that it is early-career researchers' projects of four months or more, many posted as forum posts rather than taken up by a lab. 0.8, our judgment, 0.4 to 1.2 (the family's ceiling), as Epoch AI's 0.8, below a typical project's 1.

rows.label: AI field work: share of the work no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: The share of the extension research no one else would have done now. Without MATS some alumni would have done similar research anyway (asked what they would have done that winter without MATS, 24% of the Winter 2023-24 cohort said independent research without a mentor and 13% with one, several answers allowed) or joined other programmes (the Astra fellowship, SPAR, LASR, the Anthropic Fellows), and mentors would have pursued some projects with other juniors; 78% of surveyed alumni said their publication 'possibly' or 'probably' would not have happened without MATS. Our judgment, 0.6 (0.35 to 0.85), as GovAI's and IAPS's research; that the work would have come years later is in years_of_impact.

Other AI safety research programmes (the Astra fellowship, SPAR, ERA, LASR Labs, PIBBSS) are smaller and also oversubscribed, so most of these places would not have been offered elsewhere: 0.85, our judgment, 0.7 to 1, a little below GovAI's and IAPS's 0.9 because technical safety has more substitute programmes than policy.

rows.label: AI field work: this charity's share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: MATS pays for the extension's office, housing, compute and research management (line 4b, about $1.35M with its share of management); the alumni's monthly stipends come from outside funders (the extension depends on 'securing external funding', the Apply to MATS 7.0 post; the Long-Term Future Fund, Open Philanthropy, Manifund and others), and mentors give their time. In 2024: the winter cohort's 36 extension scholars (1 April to 19 July, about 3.6 months) and the summer cohort's, on a 'funded 6 to 12 month extension' from September (no count published, our judgment of some 40 for about four months in 2024), at the main phase's $4,800 a month about $0.6M and $0.8M, $1.4M together, against MATS's $1.35M. MATS's share about half, our judgment, 30% (more outside-funded months) to 75%.

rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): no outcome of MATS's work on the risk is measured, and its alumni survey has no comparison group (who would have entered the field anyway is a judgment); every branch rests on a typical project's effect and on judgment, so $missing_data_discount.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Benefits not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Good beyond what the branches count (the scholars' research during the ten weeks is in the training branch, fb_research_dollars): the tenth of the research left out of the catastrophe chain (catastrophe_relevant_share) and work against smaller AI harms; organisations alumni founded beyond their own work-years (10% of alumni co-founded AI safety organisations or teams, the home page says); seminars and the community. 5%, our judgment, 2% to 20%, below GovAI's 15% and IAPS's 10%, which also hold their fellows' own research.

source.title: MATS, home page
source.quote: 10% of our alumni have co-founded AI safety organizations and research teams

rows.label: Harm: speeding up dangerous capabilities, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Beyond a typical project's backfire (in the shared cut): MATS trains people in empirical ML research on frontier models and is a pipeline into frontier labs (alumni join Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI, mostly on safety teams), where safety work also helps the labs build and ship more capable systems, and some alumni move to capabilities work (1.4% of surveyed alumni; more would not say so in a safety programme's survey). -7%, our judgment, down to -20%, more than the Center for AI Safety's -5%, IAPS's -5% and FAR.AI's -3% because it adds researchers to the labs directly.

source.title: MATS Alumni Impact Analysis (LessWrong, 30 September 2024)
source.quote: 1.4% are "Working/interning on AI capabilities."

rows.label: Harm: information hazards and attention, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Beyond a typical project's backfire: the evaluations stream publishes dangerous-capability evaluations and some scholars publish jailbreaks and attacks on safeguards, which can show misusers a path; most of the work is on alignment, interpretability and oversight, with nothing sensitive published. -1%, our judgment, down to -5%, as IAPS's, below GovAI's -3% and FAR.AI's -5% for threat models and working attacks.
